name: Word Studies

objectives.text: Identify key Bible words such as grace, sin, and faith when a teacher reads a passage aloud
Use a picture Bible dictionary or glossary to find what a Bible word means
Use the surrounding sentences of a verse to explain what a key word means in that passage
Use an English concordance to locate other verses that use the same word
Explain that the Bible was first written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek and that English Bibles are translations of those words
Summarize the meaning of key doctrinal terms such as justification, adoption, and sanctification as the Reformed catechisms define them
Compare how one English word is used in different verses to show that a word can carry different meanings
Explain from Scripture why careful attention to individual words matters for understanding God's Word
Use Strong's numbers to identify the Hebrew or Greek word behind an English word in a passage
Explain why different English translations may render the same Hebrew or Greek word with different English words
Analyze the semantic range of a word and select the meaning that best fits a particular passage
Interpret a word according to how a specific biblical author uses it in his own writings
Distinguish the Greek words for love in their contexts without overstating the difference between them
Explain the root fallacy and why a word's etymology does not determine its meaning in a passage
Identify common word study errors such as reading later meanings back into a word or importing every possible meaning into one verse
Use a standard lexicon and theological wordbook to gather the range of meanings for a Hebrew or Greek word
Construct a basic word study on a key theological term by moving from concordance search to context to a supported definition
Evaluate how a word's use in the Septuagint informs its meaning in the New Testament
Defend the importance of precise definitions in theology using the Reformed understanding of justify as declare righteous
Evaluate a published word study or sermon illustration for accurate use of the original languages
Produce a study of a biblical concept across an author's writings that distinguishes the concept from any single word used for it

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies: identifying key words, dictionary use, comparing usage, original languages, catechism definitions, Strong's numbers, semantic range, author usage, agape, root fallacy, constructing a study, Septuagint, precise definitions, concept study. Dropped filler such as 'recall that words mean special things' and folded 'same word in different places' into concordance and comparison objectives. Added context clues, English concordance use, translation variation, scriptural basis for attention to words, other word study fallacies, lexicon use, and evaluating published word studies. Replaced vague references with passages that model each skill and added Westminster and Heidelberg citations only where they define the doctrine or term taught.
